newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S. Africa invites bid for 20-30 pct Telkom stake.
newsitem.headline: S. Africa invites bid for 20-30 pct Telkom stake.

text.p: The South African government has now formally invited four potential buyers to submit detailed bids for a 20 to 30 percent stake in the state-owned Telkom utility, Telecommunications Minister Jay Naidoo said on Monday.
Naidoo told Reuters the request for proposal (RFP) went out on schedule in the first week of December, listing parameters for the country's first significant privatisation move.
"We said the RFP would go out in the first week of December and it did," he said.

Telecommunications Ministry spokesman Connie Malusi said the Telkom bid request was sent separately last Wednesday to Deutsche Telkom and France Telecom and to Telekom Malaysia and South Western Bell of the United States, who announced a month ago they would bid as a consortium.
"We have heard that Deutsche Telekom and France Telecom are talking to each other about bidding as a consortium, but we have not heard any details," he said.
He added detailed bids were expected by the end of January and the government would announce a deal by the end of March.

"The request for proposal spells out the bidding criteria. It outlines our vision and the objectives of the restructuring operation and gives an indication of the targets we would hope to meet," he said.
"It also sets out what the valuation criteria will be."

Malusi said the 200-page invitation called for proposals on service extension to black communities neglected under apartheid, on management expertise and training and on technical training and technology transfer.

Though almost all whites have home telephones, South Africa has fewer than one telephone for every eight people. Telkom has undertaken to deliver two million new telephone lines and to upgrade a further one million in the next five years.

Malusi said the guaranteed exclusivity period for fixed-line voice services without commercial competition would be decided in further negotiation, but would remain within the four to six year range initially set by Naidoo.

President Nelson Mandela is expected later this week to name six members to the council of a proposed telecommunications regulatory authority, which will oversee the development of the industry and manage licensing.
Malusi said the council would be consulted on the terms of a licence for the state-owned Telkom corporation, including the duration of the guaranteed monopoly for fixed-line voice telephony.

Naidoo has said previously he hopes the Telkom deal will raise between five and six billion rand in cash and an equivalent amount in non-cash contributions to the expansion of South Africa's post-apartheid telecommunications network.
Some of the money could be used to redeem state debt, and will not necessarily be used to finance the development of the telecommunications infrastructure.
The Telkom deal is the first major step in the promised restructuring of state-owned facilities inherited from the former white government.

Other utilities identified as possible targets for total or partial privatisation include the regional Sun Air airline, South African Airways, state-owned holiday resorts and parts of the Eskom power utility.
